A DECADE OF HOLISTIC TRANSFORMATION  Great universities are not built one structure at a time. They are shaped through a vision where every element grows together, creating something far greater than the sum of its parts. For ten remarkable years, NSBM Green University has transformed with purpose, continuously expanding its landscape of opportunity through world-class learning spaces, pioneering research facilities, modern laboratories, centres of innovation, sporting excellence, vibrant social environments and sustainable infrastructure. Every expansion has been matched by consistent high performance, proving that growth has never come at the expense of excellence. Instead, every new development has strengthened the University’s ability to deliver outstanding academic standards, foster innovation and create an environment where progress is both purposeful and enduring. Together, these interconnected spaces have formed a dynamic ecosystem that continues to redefine the benchmark for higher education in Sri Lanka. This holistic transformation has established NSBM as more than a place of higher learning. It has become a destination where innovation meets ambition, infrastructure empowers ideas and every advancement reinforces a culture of excellence. As the University enters its second decade, it does so with the confidence that transformation is never complete. Every new horizon presents another opportunity to elevate performance, strengthen its legacy and continue shaping one of Sri Lanka’s most progressive educational institutions.

ANOTHER CHAPTER OF OUR PROGRESS  A Decade of Value Creation towards Another Decade of  Progress  NSBM enters its second decade in 2026; the past decade has been a true and honest reflection of our bold ambitions, pursued with disciplined, well-planned activities and detailed execution. We have clearly achieved our goal of establishing a world- class green university town; not only has it emboldened our focus on environmental sustainability, but it has also become a haven of learning and professional growth for thousands of future-ready undergraduates and graduates. Over the past decade, we have grown from a concept to an institution of great national importance that seeks to achieve globally based aspirations for our students and stakeholders, and for the nation’s future. With bolder plans and bigger aspirations guiding us into the future, we welcome you to step into our next decade of growth.  Dear readers and stakeholders,  We extend our greetings to you as you take a journey through the second Integrated Annual Report of the NSBM Group. We present this year’s report with the assurance that it provides comprehensive and transparent information on how we have completed another Financial Year of stakeholder-driven value creation and financial growth.  REPORTING SCOPE  We bring your attention to our transition from a Limited Liability Company to a Guarantee Ltd. in the previous financial year. Due to this shift, our previous annual report covered an eight and a half month period. However, we have once again realigned our focus to a 12-month reporting cycle, spanning from 1st April 2025 to 31st March 2026.  4 ABOUT NSBM   YEAR IN REVIEW   STAKEHOLDER IMPACT & VALUE CREATION   CAPITAL MANAGEMENT  NSBM GROUP   ANNUAL REPORT 2025/26  ABOUT THE REPORT

GOVERNANCE AND COMPLIANCE   FUTURE OUTLOOK   FINANCIAL REPORTS   SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION 7 A DECADE OF HOLISTIC TRANSFORMATION  NSBM GREEN UNIVERSITY – INSTITUTIONAL PROFILE  NSBM Green University has grown into one of Sri Lanka’s most forward-thinking, multi-disciplined higher education institutions. Over the past 10 years, NSBM has been guided by a clear focus on its priorities: academic excellence, a strong focus on sustainability and meaningful engagements with industries. These core principles have guided NSBM’s journey and will continue to influence its decisions and operations. Chronological Milestones 2011 Foundation - Launched as a national strategic vision. Incorporated under the Companies Act No. 7 of 2007. 2012 First Cohort - Opened NSBM City Campus and welcomed inaugural undergraduates. 2013 The Rs 10.2 Bn Mega- Investment - Laid the foundation for the Homagama sustainable university town. 2016 The Green Landmark - Commenced operations as South Asia’s first regional Green University. Present Full Accreditation - Recognised degree-awarding institution under the Universities Act (Section 25A).  NSBM was founded with a simple yet ambitious objective: to prepare our young students to be confident stakeholders and leaders on the global stage, grounded in responsibility and integrity. Staying true to this vision, NSBM has steadily and strongly built a reputation as a modern and ground-breaking institution that has become a benchmark for national and regional higher education in South Asia. A defining part of its identity is being positioned and recognised as the first regional green university, which reflects an honest commitment to protecting and working around the environment, while supporting sustainable development.  ORIGIN AND PROGRESSION  NSBM commenced in 2011 as a vision that has now flourished into a national ambition. The Campus is now a fully- fledged, globally-aligned university, known as a ‘knowledge village’, raising the standards of higher education in Sri Lanka. Upon obtaining necessary approvals and registrations, in 2012, NSBM opened its doors with the NSBM City Campus, which welcomed its initial cohort of undergraduates. In 2013, the foundation was laid for the construction of a purpose-built and sustainability-conscious university town in Homagama, supported by an investment of Rs 10.2 Bn. The Campus reached its most significant milestone in 2016 when operations commenced at the sprawling University Town. At present, NSBM has risen to the level of a degree-awarding institution, recognised and accredited by the Ministry of Education under Section 25A of the Universities Act No. 16 of 1978.

The faculty offers a comprehensive portfolio of undergraduate, postgraduate, professional, and executive programmes designed to meet the evolving needs of a carefully selected student body.  Committed to academic excellence, innovation, and research, the faculty nurtures future business leaders through a premium learning experience supported by highly qualified academic staff and industry experts. While maintaining full responsibility for the academic standards and quality of its programmes, the faculty enhances students’ learning experiences through strategic partnerships with leading global business schools, providing valuable international exposure and perspectives. Recognising the challenges of digitalisation, globalisation, and changing demographic trends, the Faculty of Business delivers market-oriented and transdisciplinary study programmes that prepare graduates to thrive in an increasingly complex and competitive business environment. Driven by a culture of excellence and continuous improvement, the faculty continually evolves to reflect the changing demands of the global business landscape and to produce graduates who are globally competent, innovative, and industry-ready. At NSBM, business education extends beyond the classroom. Students are exposed to real-world business practices and experiences alongside theoretical learning, enabling them to develop strong analytical, critical-thinking, and problem-solving skills. This practical approach ensures that graduates are well equipped to meet the challenges of the modern business world with confidence and professionalism. The Faculty of Business places great emphasis on providing students with intellectual depth, abundant learning resources, personalised attention, and opportunities for holistic development, creating an enriching educational experience that supports both academic and professional success.

36 ABOUT NSBM   YEAR IN REVIEW   STAKEHOLDER IMPACT & VALUE CREATION   CAPITAL MANAGEMENT  NSBM GROUP   ANNUAL REPORT 2025/26  FACULTIES AND ACADEMIC PORTFOLIO  ACADEMIC PORTFOLIO AND PARTNERSHIPS  The Department of Management offers a broad portfolio of academic pathways spanning both local and international business education. It currently delivers the Foundation Programme for Bachelor’s Degree, together with MOHE-approved programmes in Human Resource Management and International Business offered by NSBM Green University. These programmes give students a strong  grounding in management knowledge,  business practice, leadership, people  management, global business and  organisational decision-making. Beyond its local degrees, the Department contributes to NSBM’s international academic portfolio through transnational education partnerships. These include the BSc (Hons) International Management and  Business with the University of Plymouth, United Kingdom; the Bachelor of Business  (Management and Innovation & Supply Chain and Logistics Management) with  Victoria University, Australia; the Bachelor  of Science in Business Administration  (BSBA) with American University, USA; and the Bachelor of Business with Southern  Cross University, Australia.  Module coverage across these  pathways reflects the practical needs of undergraduate business education, introducing students to both foundational management knowledge and applied business skills. The emphasis is on connecting theory with organisational practice through case discussions, presentations, group-based research, guest sessions and supervised student activities, with modules and degree content kept current through engagement with industry experts and company round tables. This portfolio reflects the Department’s contribution to NSBM Green University’s wider objective of producing graduates who are academically sound, professionally prepared and capable of responding to the changing expectations of local and global business environments.  STUDENT ENGAGEMENT AND EMPLOYABILITY DEVELOPMENT  The Human Resources Unit supports the Department’s work in HRM education and contributes to developing graduates with knowledge of people management, employment relations, professional behaviour and organisational effectiveness. The International Business Management Unit supports the Department’s international business programmes by  focusing on global business environments,  internationalisation, cultural awareness,  market dynamics and cross-border business  decision-making. Both units contribute to academic delivery while also supporting discipline-based student engagement. Much of the Department’s student development is driven by its five student-led subject circles; the Human Resource Circle, the International Business Management Circle, the Entrepreneurship Circle and the Young Researchers’ Circle and Public Relations Circle. Supervised by academic staff, these circles give students structured responsibility for planning events, coordinating teams, managing timelines and engaging with industry, complementing classroom learning by building leadership, teamwork, communication, analytical  thinking, research awareness and  professional confidence. The Human Resource Circle sustained the Department’s industry connection through EXQUIZITE, its flagship corporate quiz, positioned as the largest such corporate quiz competition organised by a university in the country. The circle also delivered graduate-facing initiatives such  as the FOOTPRINTS HR Alumni Forum, interview-readiness webinars and sessions  on professional branding, LinkedIn profile building and CV preparation, supporting students ahead of internships and early- career opportunities. The International Business Management Circle continued to strengthen students’ exposure to global business knowledge and practice through a range of student-led academic initiatives. Its activities included GlobalBizX, an academic competition  designed to enhance awareness of  international business concepts, and Mind scape, a multi-round competition that engaged students with international business cases, global business practices, international business leaders, problem-  solving tasks and decision-making  challenges. These activities encouraged students to apply classroom learning in interactive and practical settings while developing analytical thinking, teamwork, communication and future-ready graduate attributes. The Circle also contributed to wider university-level initiatives, including senior orientation and Campus- to-Corporate career guidance activities, providing its members with valuable experience in event coordination, cross- functional collaboration and engagement with faculty units and student bodies. Entrepreneurial learning remained an important area of departmental engagement, with the Entrepreneurship Circle creating opportunities for students to explore entrepreneurship beyond classroom learning. Its activities included the Future Biztycoon workshop series, student entrepreneur development programmes,  business idea discussions, Global  Entrepreneurship Week activities, and contributions to wider university initiatives  such as EMERGE and sessions on women in  entrepreneurship. Through these initiatives, students were exposed to key areas such as business modelling, product-market fit, pitching, customer understanding, market validation, communication and resilience.  By engaging in founder stories, industry  perspectives and peer-led enterprise initiatives, the Department encouraged students to view entrepreneurship as a practical and evolving process that connects creativity, opportunity recognition and business execution.  RESEARCH AND KNOWLEDGE DEVELOPMENT  Research development remained a key area of progress for the Department, supported through undergraduate research engagement, staff research contributions and discipline-focused academic activities. The Department of Management Student Research Symposium provided undergraduates with a formal platform to present research, receive academic feedback and develop awareness of the standards expected in academic

This publication arrives at a historic and deeply meaningful milestone for our university: the celebration of our 10th anniversary. We find ourselves standing at a magnificent  crossroads as NSBM Green University  marks a decade. Looking back across the landscape of the last ten years, I am both humbled and proud to reflect on a journey defined by unyielding resilience, bold innovation, and a beautifully shared vision. What began as an ambitious initiative to redefine higher education in Sri Lanka has now grown into a dynamic national institution with a strong global outlook. VISION AND INCEPTION  NSBM Green University was born out of a  simple yet powerful vision: to open doors for Sri Lankan students who aspire to earn a world-class education right here on home soil. This vision directly addressed a critical national challenge. Every year, our national  university system faces the heartbreaking reality of being unable to accommodate all who qualify, leaving thousands of talented  young minds without a clear pathway to higher studies locally. Historically, this forced many families to seek opportunities  overseas, draining local talent and  household savings. NSBM fundamentally changed that reality. We became the bridge connecting youthful ambition with genuine local opportunity. In 2011, National School of Business Management Ltd. (NSBM) was established under the Companies Act, with institutional oversight by the Ministry of Education. NSBM project was based on 4 objectives.     To make a substantial impact on the higher education ratio of Sri Lanka by providing opportunities for school leavers to pursue higher education     To cater to human resource  development of the country by making globally competitive graduates suited to  industry demand     To save foreign exchange by retaining  students who are leaving for higher  education in other countries by giving an international university experience and programmes     To attract foreign students to study in  Sri Lanka, aligning with the vision of making Sri Lanka the knowledge hub in the region and, by doing that to earn  foreign exchange for the country The development of the university infrastructure was initiated with the strategic acquisition of 26 acres of land in Pitipana, Homagama. The financial  architecture was anchored by an LKR  8.6 billion loan from the Bank of Ceylon. Importantly, no government budgetary allocations were utilised. In early 2012, while construction of the NSBM Green University complex was still underway, NSBM City Campus was launched in Nugegoda. This strategic move ensured brand continuity and enabled early revenue generation, serving as a bridge between concept and full-scale implementation. Over its four-year operation, the City Campus not only performed remarkably well but also affirmed the viability and relevance of NSBM’s academic model. With consistent profitability and growing student  enrollment, it greatly enhanced NSBM’s  brand value and institutional credibility. This early success served as a vital proof of concept, instilling confidence in key stakeholders—including government bodies, financial institutions, and international academic partners—and laying a strong foundation for the ambitious university town project that was to follow. The construction of NSBM Green University was completed in an impressive  100 days, guided by a forward-thinking,  environmentally conscious master plan. The campus was designed with sustainable features and a with “green” concept,  symbolising the university’s commitment  to sustainable development, mainly aligned with SDG 4 (Quality Education), SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure), and SDG 13 (Climate Action).  Academically, the university was launched  with a dual mandate: delivering globally recognized, industry-relevant degrees that harmonize uncompromising excellence with true affordability. While overseas higher education pathways often come with staggering financial barriers, we have stayed fiercely true to our promise: providing international-standard education through accessible, value-driven pathways. By keeping this calibre of education within reach, we do more than just serve today’s students; we play a vital role in protecting Sri Lanka's economy by reducing foreign currency outflow and supporting the nation’s transformation into a regional hub for knowledge, research, and innovation. For NSBM, the impact was primarily reflected in higher operating costs, imported educational resources, and increased emphasis on financial support for students. NSBM continued to strengthen operational soundness through sound financial management, digital transformation, diversified international partnerships, and a continued focus on providing high-quality education amid evolving global instabilities.  Risk   Impact on NSBM   Key Mitigating Measures Rising Energy and Operating Costs  Increased utility, transport and campus operating expenses due to global energy price volatility. Continuous monitoring of operating costs, adoption of energy-efficient campus programs, and optimisation of non- essential expenditure through regular budget reviews.  Inflation and Student Affordability  Higher living costs may affect student enrolment, retention, and timely fee payments. Financial assistance programmes, together with proactive student involvement to support retention.  Foreign Exchange Volatility   Increased costs of software licences, imported equipment and overseas academic activities. Advance budgeting for foreign currency commitments, prioritisation of essential international expenditure, and greater use of digital engagement with overseas partners.  Supply Chain Disruptions   Delays in sourcing laboratory equipment, IT infrastructure and academic materials. Early procurement planning, supplier diversification, and maintaining adequate inventories of critical teaching and research resources.  Cybersecurity and Business Continuity Risks  Increased danger of cyberattacks and disruption to academic and administrative operations.  Strengthening cybersecurity controls, regular system  backups, staff awareness programmes, and implementation of business continuity and disaster recovery procedures.

Members of the QASDC are tasked with ensuring that all NSBM academic programs, teaching methods, and staff development programs complement national and globally recognised quality standards. WEERASINGHE  Vice-Chancellor & Chief Executive Officer  Prof. E. A. Weerasinghe is a visionary leader and distinguished academic who has significantly transformed the higher education landscape in Sri Lanka. Driven by a steadfast dedication to empowering the nation's youth, Prof. Weerasinghe  embarked on a mission to establish a  pioneering educational institute, offering an unparalleled higher education experience with world-class opportunities.  Throughout his illustrious career as an  academic, educational administrator, entrepreneur, and transformative leader, Prof. Weerasinghe has gained notable recognition for his expertise in management development and training, productivity improvement, and management consultancy. His career reached a pivotal point when he became the Director General of the National Institute of Business Management (NIBM). Under his leadership, the institute was transformed into a modern, financially prosperous entity within just five years. During his tenure at NIBM, Prof. Weerasinghe envisioned creating a higher education institution that would provide aspiring young learners with the opportunity to pursue their academic dreams. This vision led to the creation of the NSBM (National  School of Business Management) Green  University. Situated on a 26-acre landscape in the idyllic Homagama town near Colombo, the inception of NSBM marked a significant milestone in higher education with its green campus concept, reminiscent of the experiences at Cambridge and Oxford, as detailed in the NSBM Corporate Plan. The design aimed to offer a comprehensive university experience with exceptional facilities, innovative programs, and a dedicated human resources department. Under Prof. Weerasinghe's visionary leadership, the NSBM Green University Complex was established in 2016. Today,  NSBM thrives with over 12,000 students  and more than five programs. Built with an investment of Rs. 10.2 billion, this self- financed entity operates under the Ministry of Education without imposing any financial burden on the government. Prof. Weerasinghe's unwavering commitment, pioneering spirit, and visionary leadership have propelled NSBM toward its goal of positioning Sri Lanka as the leading inclusive growth center of Asia. This revolutionary institute has transformed the lives of countless students, equipping  them with the knowledge, skills, and  mindset necessary to excel in their chosen fields. As the Vice-Chancellor of NSBM, Prof. Weerasinghe continues to inspire educators, students, and policymakers,  ensuring a brighter future for higher  education in Sri Lanka. In addition to his role at NSBM, Prof. Weerasinghe is an active member of the Sri Lanka Association for the Advancement of Science and serves as a Justice of the Peace for the whole island. An esteemed academic,  he has served as the Head and Senior  Lecturer in the Departments of Business Economics and Public Administration at the University of Sri Jayewardenepura, supervising numerous undergraduate and postgraduate research projects. He is also an accomplished author of numerous national and international journal papers and research articles, with research interests in Multinational Enterprises & Economic Development and the Economic Impact of uncontrollable natural events. Prof. Weerasinghe holds a BA (Special)  in Economics from the University of  Sri Jayewardenepura, a Postgraduate Diploma in Development Economics from the University of Colombo, an M.Sc. in Computing from Bradford University, UK, an M.Sc. in Economics from Wakayama University, Japan, and a Doctorate in Economics from Osaka City University, Japan. In 2016, he was honoured at the "Jayawardenepura Pradeepa" Annual Awards Ceremony by the Alumni Association of the University of Sri Jayewardenepura. In recognition of his outstanding contributions, Prof. Weerasinghe has been honoured with numerous national and international awards, including:     Jayawardene Pradeepa Pranama Award (2016) – Presented by the Alumni Association of the University of Sri Jayewardenepura to a select group of distinguished alumni in honour of their remarkable contributions to national development.     Janabhimani Honorary Award (2019) – Helaye Mahaviru Ravana Rajabhimani  Gold Award, conferred by the All  Ceylon Free Journalists’ Association in recognition of his pioneering leadership in establishing NSBM Green University.     Most Outstanding Citizen Award (2024) – Presented by Lions International in appreciation of his exceptional and sustained contributions to society.     Global CEO Leadership Excellence Award (2024) – Awarded by Global CEO Magazine for demonstrating transformative leadership on a global scale.     JaGAAS Lifetime Achievement Award – Presented by the Japanese Graduates’ Alumni Association of Sri Lanka (JaGAAS) in recognition of his significant contributions to the nation as a distinguished alumnus of Japanese universities.     The Most Visionary Leader Award  (2025) – Bestowed by the Federation of Chambers of Commerce and Industry of Sri Lanka (FCCISL) at the Sri Lankan Entrepreneur of the Year Awards  (SLEOTY), recognising his far-sighted  leadership.     Gold Award – National Extra-Large Category and Gold Award – Western Province Extra-Large Category (2025) – Presented by FCCISL at SLEOTY in recognition of his exceptional entrepreneurship and organisational excellence. Prof. E. A. Weerasinghe’s legacy stands as a beacon of excellence, innovation, and national pride—an enduring testament to the transformative power of visionary leadership in higher education.

INTERNAL GOVERNANCE THE BOARD  At NSBM Green University, the Board serves as the university’s guiding force,  entrusted with crucial responsibilities. It spearheads the approval of strategic directives, diligently oversees the university’s progress and management performance, and cultivates an environment conducive to achieving our strategic goals. Primarily, the Board shoulders the pivotal tasks of defining strategic trajectories, green lighting financial plans and significant initiatives, vigilantly monitoring university performance, ensuring robust risk management practices, endorsing commercial endeavours, and supervising academic affairs. By maintaining a significant proportion of independent voices on the board, we uphold the highest standards of governance, transparency, and integrity, thus fostering an environment conducive to effective  oversight and strategic guidance for NSBM  Green University. GENERAL MEETINGS  NSBM holds an Annual General Meeting (AGM) each year. AUDIT AND MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE  The Audit and Management Committee is responsible for monitoring the ongoing effectiveness of risk management activities. The committee monitors trends in the university’s risk profile and considers how it manages or mitigates key risk exposures. The university implements risk management through its business processes of planning, budgeting, investment and project analysis, and operations management, and uses internal audit processes and project post-implementation reviews to monitor performance in various areas. The committee also monitors and oversees the quality of financial reporting and financial management. To achieve this, the committee considers accounting and audit issues, makes recommendations to the Council as required, and monitors the role, responsibility, and performance of the internal and external auditors. The function of the Audit and Management Committee is to assist the Board in carrying out its responsibilities pursuant to legislation on matters relating to the university’s accounting practices, policies and controls relevant to the financial position and to liaise with internal and external auditors on behalf of the Board.  INTERNAL AUDIT  The role of the university’s Internal Audit  function is to provide an independent, objective assurance and consulting service that adds value and improves operations. The audit function achieves this through a systematic and disciplined approach to evaluating and improving risk management, control, and governance processes. The function operates under the internal  audit reviews conducted quarterly by  the Audit & Management Committee. Significant risks identified during audits and audit recommendations are notified to  university management and the Audit and  Management Committee in a timely manner to enable management to take appropriate remedial action. Mitigating actions  undertaken to address risks and internal  audit recommendations are followed up monthly by Internal Audit to ensure timely implementation. THE SENATE  To provide a glimpse of the historical development of the concept of the Senate, from ancient times in Scotland and other universities, the Senate was responsible for authorising degree programs, issuing  degrees to grandaunts and honorary  recipients, and for the discipline of students. All scholastic units of the university were members of the Senate for the systematic maintenance of the core function of the Senate. S. 46 of the Sri Lankan Universities Act provides for the establishment of the Senate at universities. The establishment of an  academic governing body at NSBM Green  University can be identified as a pivotal milestone identified in the strategic plan of the institution for good, responsible,  and equitable governance at NSBM Green  University. The Senate is the supreme academic body  for Academic Governance at NSBM Green  University. The core function of the Senate is to regulate and superintend the teaching and discipline, oversight, and regulation of the academic provisions of NSBM, and to promote research at NSBM Green University. It will ensure and maintain the academic standards of the institution and fulfil the requirements and expectations of external authorities and agencies, particularly the Quality Assurance Council of the University Grants Commission, according to the Sri Lanka Qualification Framework, research Councils, and  Professional, Statutory and Regulatory  Bodies. The permanent members of the Senate include the Vice-Chancellor, Deputy Vice-Chancellor, Head of Academic Development and Quality Assurance, Deans of the five faculties, Heads of Departments and Academic Units, Senior Professorial staff members, one elected academic staff member from each faculty (non- professorial) of NSBM Green University, two external representatives representing the industry and Registrar/ Secretary to the Senate. Apart from the main positions, the Head of Finance, Senior Manager - Administration & HR, Registrar - Examination, and Head of Research Council will be performing the observer’s role in the Senate. Including these positions, a maximum of 100 members are allowed to be a part of the Senate.  The second week of every month, the Senate will be summoned under the  guidance of the Vice- Chancellor. The Vice-Chancellor possesses the power to appoint a convener to the Senate who will be responsible for convening the Senate meeting every month, circulating the agenda, circulating meeting minutes, and other reports or proposals among the  Senate members before the minutes are  confirmed at the Senate meeting. The functions of the Senate can be stated under the following points.     Approval of schemes of reorganisation of existing faculties and departments  of study     Organisation of new faculties and new departments of studies     Formal approval of the introduction of new degree programs, award of  university degrees, including honorary degrees     Formal approval of new academic ventures in faculties     Approval of the conferment of Emeritus status on retiring professors of the  university     Setting the academic regulatory  framework (delegated to the Academic  Development and Quality Assurance  Division)     Maintenance of the quality and standards of the university’s awards (delegated to the Academic  Development and Quality Assurance  Division)     Setting the high-level policy and  strategy on learning, teaching and  curriculum development working within the strategic direction contained within the university’s Strategic Plan approved  by the Board of Directors and its  underlying strategies.     Approval of By-Laws     Determination of grave student disciplinary matters     Regulating the conduct of students at the university (via the Code of Student Conduct)     Communication, assessment and approval or rejection of policies formulated by Senate Committees.     The award of fellowships, scholarships, medals, and/ or prizes     The approval of the final grandaunt lists for the convocation ceremony.     The appointment of a number of standing committees as may be deemed fit.     The approval of the list of admissions to academic degree programs     Formal approval for any other academic or academic-related activity Apart from the above-mentioned functions, the Senate has the power to appoint standing committees for academic development and quality assurance purposes. As with most institutions, risks are inherent in all activities; NSBM Green University undertakes new risks in pursuit of its strategic objectives. Effective risk management is about ensuring all significant, relevant risks are understood and prioritised as part of standard management practice to increase the probability of successful outcomes, while protecting NSBM Green University’s reputation and sustainability.  To create long-term value, we must anticipate the risks threatening our university, customers and stakeholders, whilst still capitalising on new opportunities offered by an ever-changing world. We must maintain a dialogue with internal and external stakeholders to identify those risks and opportunities. These are illustrated in our Risk Register, which includes vital business and sector risks, as well as some specific to NSBM Green University and key customers and stakeholders.  PROCESS OF NSBM GREEN UNIVERSITY  Our Board of Directors has delegated authority to the Audit and Management  Committee to oversee risk management.  This ongoing review enables NSBM Green  University to identify material issues that are most likely to affect value creation, strategic objectives, service delivery and assets. We undertake a systematic and methodical identification of key risks and identify measures to mitigate them. Whilst risk cannot be eliminated completely, the approach of the Audit and Management Committee is to be ‘risk aware’ rather than  ‘risk adverse’, by taking intelligent risks to  protect strategic objectives. RISK MANAGEMENT APPROACH  NSBM's risk management approach seeks  to increase the likelihood of achieving  the University's strategic objectives by systematically identifying material uncertainties, assessing their potential impact and likelihood, implementing appropriate mitigating controls and monitoring changes in risk exposure.  Risk management is not intended to  eliminate all risk. Sustainable growth, innovation and institutional development necessarily involve informed risk-taking.  NSBM therefore seeks to ensure that risks  associated with strategic opportunities are  understood, evaluated and managed within  an acceptable level of risk appetite. The principal risks are considered with reference to their potential impact on:     Academic quality and student  experience     Financial sustainability     People and wellbeing     Infrastructure and assets     Operational continuity     Regulatory compliance     Environment and society     Institutional reputation  UNDERSTANDING RISK IMPACT  NSBM recognises that individual risks rarely  operate in isolation. Financial, strategic, operational, technological, environmental and people-related risks are interconnected and may ultimately affect the reputation and sustainability of the University. Accordingly, reputational impact sits at the centre of NSBM's risk framework. For example, a cybersecurity incident may initially represent an operational and  technology risk but could subsequently  result in financial loss, disruption to academic activities, regulatory exposure, GOVERNANCE AND COMPLIANCE   FUTURE OUTLOOK   FINANCIAL REPORTS   SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION  279 A DECADE OF HOLISTIC TRANSFORMATION

MEETINGS OF THE AUDIT COMMITTEE  The committee met three times during the financial period ended as at 31.03.2026. Detailed reports on the proceedings and matters discussed were reported to the Board. The findings of the committee are regularly reported to the Board of Directors through the minutes of meetings. The Deputy Vice Chancellor, Dean from a Faculty, Senior Manager Administration and Head of Finance attended these meetings by invitation.  REPORTING OF FINANCIAL STATEMENTS  The Audit and Management Committee review the financial statements before presenting them to the Board of Directors. The committee assisted the Board in overseeing the preparation, presentation, and adequacy of disclosure in the financial  statements in accordance with Sri Lanka  Accounting Standards and Companies Act No 07 of 2007. This involved the review  and discussion of both annual and quarterly  financial statements, ensuring transparency and accuracy in financial reporting.  INTERNAL CONTROL AND RISK MANAGEMENT  The internal controls within the university  are designed to offer reasonable, though  not absolute, assurance to the Board of  Directors, assisting them in monitoring the Company's financial position. INTERNAL AUDIT  Internal audit reports are submitted to the committee and audit findings presented in the reports are prioritised based on the risk levels. REVIEW OF INTERNAL AUDIT FINDINGS  Throughout the year, the committee diligently reviewed internal audit findings, addressing deficiencies and implementing corrective actions. EXTERNAL AUDITORS  Messrs KPMG served as the external auditor for the 2025/2026 financial year, providing an independent assessment of the university’s financial statements. FUTURE OUTLOOK

The future of NSBM is being redefined as we develop strategies and pursue avenues to function as a catalyst for national development through academics and professional development for our youth. We have also entered the next strategic phase of transformation through academic expansion, healthcare innovation, research, sustainability, and contributions to the national workforce and economic growth.  A significant approach of our future vision is the Phase II and Phase III Campus Development and the proposed Medical and Research Hospital, which is expected to support the nation’s human capital development. Importantly, this will stimulate industry-academic collaboration, expand access to health services, and  transform NSBM into a knowledge-  oriented growth hub. The following developments collectively exemplify our long-term commitment to creating future-ready graduates. Our efforts are also expected to attract local and foreign partnerships and investments, create employment opportunities and create the resources and people needed  to deliver sustainable social and economic  value to Sri Lanka.  PHASE II  The second phase of development   represents   a significant scaling of institutional capacity and economic influence through targeted infrastructure expansion and service enhancement. This includes developing new academic   faculties (Faculty of Science and Faculty of Engineering)   and administrative facilities, specialised infrastructure such  as   civil   engineering laboratories, a   2,000-  seat auditorium, and expanded student service amenities, including cafeterias. The development also includes supporting infrastructure and campus enhancements such as a large playground, pavilion, student parking facilities, walking paths, rainwater harvesting systems, a pond,   an open   gym,   outdoor student parks, and extensive landscaping.   Collectively, these developments are expected to materially enhance the institution’s ability to  accommodate a larger student body and  deliver more diversified academic offerings. The expansion of physical infrastructure has immediate implications for the construction and capital investment ecosystem. During the development period, demand increases for construction services, engineering consultancy, materials supply,   logistics, and project management services. PHASE III – HOSPITAL PROJECT  NSBM Healthcare Ltd, a wholly owned  subsidiary of the National School of  Business Management (Guarantee) Ltd,  is preparing to launch Sri Lanka’s largest  and most advanced Medical and Research  Hospital in Homagama. This 700-bed,  state-of-the-art facility will integrate world-class clinical care, advanced research,  and internationally benchmarked medical education within a single institution. This project will go beyond medical infrastructure as a hospital, with the aim of being a hub for national healthcare and innovation that addresses the country’s urgent healthcare deficiencies. With an increasing population that contracts  non-communicable diseases, the country  requires proactive and long-term focused solutions for specialised care and to  address the shortage of skilled medical  professionals. Therefore, the NSBM Hospital will:     Provide specialised, technology-enabled  clinical services that currently require  patients to travel abroad.     Retain and develop a new generation  of doctors, nurses, and allied health  professionals equipped for the demands of modern medicine.     Advance medical research focused on  Sri Lanka’s unique disease patterns and healthcare priorities.     This project builds on NSBM Green University’s proven track record,  including the successful delivery of  South Asia’s first fully fledged Green University Town on time and within budget. It will serve as a model for  vision-driven, world-class infrastructure  in Sri Lanka. Located in the rapidly developing Homagama Tech Corridor, the hospital will attract medical tourism, global partnerships, and high-end healthcare investment. It will  feature sustainable design, advanced digital  health systems, and a multidisciplinary team of local and international experts. Healing patients is not the only focus of the NSBM Medical and Research Hospital; we  are also working to create a system that will  shape the future of Sri Lankan healthcare and innovation, and inspire truly adept medical professionals and leaders. The project has gained national recognition, and its outcome will be to create lasting social, economic, and medical benefits for decades to come.  PRIVATE HEALTHCARE SECTOR OPPORTUNITY  Sri Lanka’s private healthcare sector is undergoing a phase of steady expansion, driven by multiple converging trends: rapid urbanisation, a growing middle-income population, increased health awareness, and the emergence of medical tourism. As public hospitals face capacity and infrastructure challenges, more patients are turning to private providers for timely, personalised, higher-quality care. However, despite the growth, the private healthcare landscape remains fragmented and geographically concentrated. Most of the country’s leading private hospitals and diagnostic centres are clustered around Colombo and the Western Province, leaving the rest of the country underserved. Additionally, these institutions typically  lack integrated academic and research  capabilities, which are essential for long-term clinical excellence, continuous professional development, and innovation. This presents a clear opportunity for strategic private investment in the healthcare sector—not just to expand service provision, but to transform the  ecosystem by combining clinical care,  medical education, and research under one institution. There is a growing demand for facilities that go beyond transactional healthcare to deliver comprehensive, patient-centred, and academically enriched services. NSBM Healthcare Ltd is positioned to fill this strategic void by establishing a premier private medical institution that will serve as a national and regional benchmark. The proposed facility will focus on the following objectives.     Delivering tertiary and quaternary care using state-of-the-art diagnostics, digital platforms, and minimally invasive interventions.     Integrating electronic medical records (EMRs), AI-driven diagnostics, and smart hospital infrastructure to enhance patient safety and operational efficiency. NSBM currently manages these risks  through several approaches, including the QASDC framework, inclusive HR practices,  a strong community and stakeholder  engagement approach, and compliance mechanisms. Modestly complementing SLFRS S2, we have also recognised certain physical  climate risks, such as heavy rainfall,  drainage pressure, flooding, heat stress, water demand, and landscape damage. We have also begun addressing transition  and regulatory risks linked to low-carbon  expectations, green campus standards,  environmental laws, waste and water  compliance, and emerging ESG reporting expectations, with scope for further assessments and identifications.  However, we are assessing formal sustainability and climate-related risks and  their likelihood and impact. In time, we also plan to establish mitigation actions,  monitor residual risk, and integrate SRROs  and CRROs into our enterprise risk management and financial planning. The following provides a preliminary assessment of Climate Risks that could impact NSBM’s activities and long-term objectives/value creation.  PHYSICAL CLIMATE RISKS     Intense rainfall and flooding.     Increasing temperatures and heat stress.     Changing rainfall patterns and water availability.     Extreme weather-related disruption to campus operations.     Potential impacts on landscaping, biodiversity and infrastructure.  TRANSITION RISKS     Policy and legal risks     Market risks     Financial risks     Infrastructure-related risks     Reputation risks     Enrolment risks (student recruitment)     Curriculum and strategic risks, to name the most important.  NSBM’s overall risk-management  framework provides the foundation for identifying and managing risks that may affect the achievement of institutional objectives. NSBM progressively considers  sustainability-related and climate-related  risks alongside strategic, operational, financial, regulatory, and reputational risks.     Identification   – Sustainability and climate-related risks will be identified and established through operational  monitoring, stakeholder engagement, environmental assessments, audits and  management reviews.     Assessment   – Identified matters  will be considered in terms of their  potential operational, financial, environmental and reputational consequences.     Management   – Appropriate responses will be implemented through policies, operational controls, infrastructure design, preventive maintenance, resource-efficiency initiatives and stakeholder awareness.     Monitoring   – Energy and water usage, environmental performance  and other relevant indicators will be monitored through established internal  mechanisms.     Escalation and Oversight   – Material risks are to be incorporated into the  University’s broader risk-management  and governance processes for  management and Board-level  consideration where appropriate.

CHANGES IN ACCOUNTING  STANDARDS  3.1 CHANGES IN MATERIAL  ACCOUNTING POLICIES  The Group has applied following Accounting Policies to all periods presented in these Financial Statements.  4. MATERIAL ACCOUNTING  POLICIES  The Group has consistently applied the following accounting policies to all periods presented in these financial statements and deviations if any, have been disclosed accordingly.  4.1 FOREIGN CURRENCY  TRANSACTIONS  Transactions in foreign currencies are translated to Sri Lanka Rupees at the foreign exchange rate prevailing at the date of the transaction. Monetary assets and liabilities denominated  in foreign currencies are translated to Sri  Lanka Rupees at the foreign exchange rate ruling as at the reporting date. Foreign exchange differences arising on the settlement or reporting of the Group’s monetary item at rates different from those which are initially recorded are deal within the statement of profit or loss. Non-monetary assets and liabilities  denominated in foreign currencies that are measured at fair value are translated to the  functional currency at the exchange rate at the date that the fair value was determined. Foreign currency differences arising on translation are recognized in statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income. Non-monetary assets and liabilities that  are stated at historical cost denominated in foreign currencies are translated to Sri  Lanka Rupees at the exchange rate of the transaction date.  4.2 FINANCIAL INSTRUMENTS 4.2.1 NON-DERIVATIVE  FINANCIAL ASSETS  The Group initially recognizes loans and receivables and deposits on the date that they are originated. All other financial  assets (including assets designated at fair  value through profit or loss) are recognized initially on the trade date at which the Group becomes a party to the contractual provisions of the instrument. The Group derecognises a financial asset  when the contractual rights to the cash  flows from the asset expire, or it transfers  the rights to receive the contractual cash  flows on the financial asset in a transaction in which substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership of the financial asset are transferred. Any interest in transferred financial assets that is created or retained by the Group is recognized as a separate asset or liability. Financial assets and liabilities are offset and the net amount presented in the statement of financial position when, and only when, the Group has a legal right to offset the amounts and intends either to settle on a net basis or to realize the asset and settle the liability simultaneously.

Loans and Receivables  Loans and Receivables are financial assets with fixed or determinable payments that are not quoted in an active market. (i) Trade and other receivables  Trade and other receivables comprise of  receivable from customers, advances and  deposits and prepayments.  (ii) Cash and cash equivalents  Cash and cash equivalents comprise cash in hand and balance with banks. (iii) Amount due to related parties  Amounts due to related parties comprises  the long term receivable balances from the  related companies and directors.  Borrowing costs  Borrowing costs directly attributable to the acquisition, construction, or production of a qualifying asset are capitalized as part of  the cost of that asset in accordance with  LKAS 23 - Borrowing Costs. A qualifying  asset is an asset that necessarily takes a  substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale. Capitalization of borrowing costs ceases when substantially all the activities necessary to prepare  the qualifying asset for its intended use  are completed. Other borrowing costs are recognized in the Statement of Profit or Loss in the period in which they are incurred.  4.2.2 NON-DERIVATIVE  FINANCIAL LIABILITIES  Non derivative financial liabilities are recognized initially on the trade date at which the Group becomes a party to the contractual provisions of the instrument. The Group de-recognizes a financial liability when its contractual obligations are discharged or cancelled or expire. Financial assets and liabilities are offset and the net amount presented in the statement of financial position when, and only when, the Group has a legal right to offset the amounts and intends either to settle on a net basis or to realize the asset and settle the liability simultaneously. Non-derivative financial liabilities can be classified into two categories. Namely, Fair Value through Profit or Loss and Other Financial Liabilities. Other financial liabilities comprise: Interest bearing borrowings, bank overdrafts, related party payable and trade and other payables. Such financial liabilities are recognized initially at fair value plus any directly attributable transaction costs. Subsequent to initial recognition these financial liabilities are measured at amortized cost using the effective interest method.  4.3 NON-FINANCIAL ASSETS 4.3.1 PLANT AND EQUIPMENT a) Recognition and Measurement  Items of property, plant and equipment are stated at cost less accumulated depreciation and accumulated impairment losses. Cost includes expenditures that are directly attributable to the acquisition of the asset.  The cost of self-constructed asset includes the cost of materials and direct labor, the  initial estimate, when relevant of the cost of  the dismantling and removing the items and restoring the site on which they are located  and an appropriate proportion of overheads. The cost of acquisition includes purchase cost together with any incidental expenses  incurred in bringing the assets to its working  condition for the intended use. When parts of an item of property, plant and equipment have different useful lives, they are accounted for as separate items (major components) of property, plant and equipment.  b) Subsequent Expenditure  Expenditure incurred to replace a component of an item of property, plant and equipment that is accounted for separately, including major inspection and overhaul expenditure, is capitalized. The cost of replacing part of an item of Property, Plant and Equipment is recognized in the carrying amount of the item, if it is probable that the future economic benefits embodied within the part will flow to the Group and its cost can be measured reliably. The carrying amount of the replaced part is derecognized. The cost of the day-to-day servicing of property, plant and equipment are recognized in Statement of Profit or Loss and other comprehensive income as incurred.  c) Restoration Costs  Expenditure incurred on repairs or maintenance of property, plant and equipment in order to restore or maintain the future economic benefits expected from originally assessed standard of performance is recognized as an expense when incurred.  d) Depreciation  Free hold land is not depreciated. Depreciation has been charged to the Statement of Profit or Loss on straight line basis over the estimated useful lives of each part of an item of property, plant and equipment. A financial asset is impaired if objective evidence indicates that a loss event has occurred after the initial recognition of the asset, and that the loss event had a negative effect on the estimated future cash flows of that asset that can be estimated reliably. The Group considers evidence of impairment for receivables at specific asset level. All receivables are assessed for specific impairment. An impairment loss in respect of a financial asset measured at amortized cost is calculated as the difference between its carrying amount and the present value of the estimated future cash flows discounted at the asset’s original effective interest rate. Losses are recognized in profit or loss and reflected in an allowance account against receivables. When a subsequent event causes the amount of impairment loss to decrease, the decrease in impairment loss is reversed through profit or loss.  4.4.2 NON-FINANCIAL ASSETS  The carrying amounts of the Group’s non- financial assets, other than inventories and deferred tax assets are reviewed at each reporting date to determine whether there is any indication of impairment. If any such indication exists, then the asset’s recoverable amount is estimated. An impairment loss is recognised if the carrying amount of an assets or cash generating unit (CGU) exceeds its recoverable amount. Impairment losses are recognised in the statement of comprehensive income.  The recoverable amount of an asset or cash-  generating unit is the greater of its value in use and its fair value less costs to sell. In assessing value in use, the estimated future cash flows are discounted to their present value using a pre-tax discount rate that reflects current market assessments of the time value of money and the risks specific to the asset. For the purpose of impairment testing, assets that cannot be tested individually are grouped together into the smallest group of assets that generates cash inflows from continuing use that are largely independent of the cash inflows of other assets or groups of assets. The Group’s corporate assets do not generate separate cash inflows. If there is an indication that a corporate asset may be impaired, then the recoverable amount is determined for the CGU to which the corporate asset belongs. An impairment loss is reversed if there has been a change in the estimates used to determine the recoverable amount. An impairment loss is reversed only to the extent that the asset’s carrying amount does not exceed the carrying amount that would have been determined, net of depreciation or amortization, if no impairment loss had been recognized.  4.5 NON-FINANCIAL LIABILITIES  AND PROVISIONS  4.5.1 LIABILITIES AND  PROVISIONS  Liabilities classified as Current Liabilities in the Statement of financial position are those obligations payable on demand or within one year from the reporting date. Items classified as non current liabilities are those obligations, which expire beyond a period of one year from the reporting date. All known liabilities have been accounted for in preparing the Financial Statements. Provision and liabilities are recognized when the Group has a legal or constructive obligation as a result of past events and it is probable that an outflow of economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation.  4.5.2 PROVISIONS  A provision is recognized if, as a result of a past event, the Group has a present legal or constructive obligation that can be estimated reliably, and it is probable that an outflow of economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation. Provisions are determined by discounting the expected future cash flows at a pre-tax rate that reflects current market assessments of the time value of money and the risks specific to the liability. The unwinding of the discount is recognized as finance cost. The increase in provision due to time passage is recognized as interest expense.  4.5.3. EMPLOYEE BENEFITS a) Defined Contribution Plan  A defined contribution plan is post- employment plan under which an entity pays fixed contribution into a separate entity and will have no legal or constructive obligation to pay a further amount. Obligations for contributions to defined contribution plans are recognized as an expense in statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income in the period  during which related services are rendered  by employees.  Employees Provident Fund  The Group and Employees contribute 12% and 8% respectively on the salary of each employee respectively. Said provident fund is being managed by the Central Bank of Sri Lanka.  Employee Trust Fund  The Group contributes 3% of the salary of each employee to the Employees’ Trust Fund contributions plans are recognized as an expense in the statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income as incurred.  b) Defined Benefit Plan  A defined benefit plan is a post-employment benefit plan other than a defined contribution plan. The Group is liable to pay retirement benefits under the Payment of Gratuity Act, No 12 of 1983. The liability recognized in the financial statements in respect of defined benefit plan is the present value of the defined benefit obligation as at reporting date. The defined benefit obligation plan is calculated at reporting date based on an internally generated model. Liability is not externally funded nor actuarial valued.

Contingent liabilities are possible obligations whose existence will be confirmed only by uncertain future events or present obligations where the transfer of economic benefits is not probable or cannot be reliably measured. Capital Commitments and Contingent liabilities are not recorded in the Statement of Financial Position but are disclosed unless they are remote.  4.7 ACCOUNTING FOR  INVESTMENT IN SUBSIDIARIES  Investments in subsidiaries are initially recognized at cost in the Financial Statements of the Group. Any Transaction cost relating to acquisition of investment in subsidiaries are immediately recognized in Profit or Loss. Following initial recognition,  investment in subsidiaries are carried at  cost less any accumulated impairment losses. The net assets of each subsidiary is reviewed at each reporting date to determine whether there is any indication of impairment. If any such indication exists, then the recoverable amount of the investment is estimated and the impairment loss is recognized to the extent of its net assets loss.  4.8 STATEMENT OF SURPLUS  OR DEFICIT AND OTHER COMPREHENSIVE INCOME  4.8.1 REVENUE RECOGNITION  The Group recognizes revenue in accordance with SLFRS 15 – Revenue from Contracts with Customers, using the five- step model. Revenue is recognized when control of the promised goods or services is  transferred to the customer or student, at  an amount that reflects the consideration the Group expects to be entitled to in exchange for those goods or services. Revenue is measured at the transaction price, net of discounts, concessions, taxes  collected on behalf of the government, and  any other price adjustments. All other income is recognized on accrual basis.  4.8.2 EXPENDITURE a) Operating Expenses  All expenditure incurred in the running  of the business and in maintaining the  property, plant and equipment in a state of efficiency has been charged to the statement of comprehensive income.  b) Finance Expenses  Finance expenses comprise interest expense on interest borrowings and lease interest. Interest expenses are recognized using the effective interest method.  c) Finance Income  Finance income comprise interest income derived on savings deposits. Interest income is recorded as accrues using the effective interest rate (EIR).  4.8.3 INCOME TAX EXPENSES  Tax expenses comprise current tax expenses recognized directly in the statement of comprehends of Profit or Loss except to the extent that it relate to items recognized directly in equity or other comprehensive income.  a) Current Taxation  Current tax comprises the expected tax payable or receivable on the taxable income for the year and any adjustment to tax payable or receivable in respect of the previous years. It is measured using tax rates enacted or substantively enacted in the reporting date. Current tax also includes any tax arising from dividends.  b) Deferred Tax  Deferred tax is recognized for all temporary differences arising between the tax bases of assets and liabilities and their carrying amounts in the consolidated financial statements. Deferred tax liabilities are recognized for all taxable temporary differences. Deferred tax assets are recognized for deductible temporary differences, unused tax losses, and unused tax credits to the extent that it is probable that future taxable profits will be available against which these can be utilized. The carrying amount of deferred tax assets is reviewed at each reporting date and reduced to the extent that it is no longer probable that sufficient taxable profits will be available. Unrecognised deferred tax assets are reassessed at each reporting date and recognized to the extent that it becomes probable that future taxable profits will allow recovery. Deferred tax is measured using the tax rates and tax laws enacted or substantively enacted at the reporting date that are expected to apply when the asset is realized or the liability is settled.  4.8.4 BASIC EARNINGS PER  SHARE  The Group presents basic earnings per share (EPS) data for its ordinary shares. Basic EPS is calculated by dividing the profit or loss attributable to ordinary shareholders of the Group by the weighted average  number of ordinary shares in issue during  the period.  4.8.5 RELATED PARTY  TRANSACTIONS  Disclosure has been made in respect of the transactions in which one party has the ability to control or exercise significant influence over the financial and operating policies/decisions of the other, irrespective of whether a price is being charged.  4.9 STATEMENT OF CASH FLOWS  The statement of cash flows statement has been prepared by using the “Indirect Method” of preparing of cash flow statement in accordance with LKAS 7- Cash Flow Statement. Cash and Cash equivalents comprises cash balances, deposits with banks and placements. For the purpose of cash flows,  cash and cash equivalents are shown net of  bank overdraft.

Thus, the consolidation Financial Statements present financial information about the Group as a single economic entity distinguishing the equity attributable to the parent (controlling interest) and attributable to minority shareholders with Non-Controlling Interests.  4.10.2 TRANSFERS OF  OPERATIONS  Transfers of operations within entities  under common control are accounted for at  the date on which the transferring entity’s assets, liabilities, and related activities are legally transferred to the Group. Control represents the ability to direct the financial and operating policies of an operation so as to derive benefits from its activities. In evaluating control, the Group considers rights that are currently exercisable and any governance or oversight powers held by the relevant authorities. In cases where operations or activities are transferred to the Group as part of  an internal restructuring, the assets and  liabilities received are recognized at their existing carrying amounts. No goodwill or bargain gain is recognized. Amounts relating to the settlement of any pre-existing arrangements are recognized in the statement of profit or loss at the time such obligations arise. Costs directly attributable to the restructuring or transfer are expensed as incurred, except where  they relate to the issuance of debt or equity  instruments.  If the transfer arrangement includes  deferred or conditional payments, the related payable is recorded at the present value of the expected future payments. Subsequent adjustments to this liability are recognized in the statement of profit or loss unless the liability is classified as equity, in which case changes are recognized within equity.  4.10.3 SUBSIDIARIES  Subsidiaries are entities controlled by the Group. The Group controls an entity if it is exposed to, or has rights to, variable returns from its involvement with the entity and has the ability to affect those returns through its power over the entities.  The Financial Statements of subsidiaries  are included in the Consolidated Financial  Statements from the date that control  effectively commences until the date that control effectively ceases. The Financial Statements of all companies in the Group have a common financial year which ends on 31 March. Where Subsidiaries have been sold or acquired during the year, their operating  results have been included to the date of  disposal or from the date of acquisition. Upon the loss of control, the Group derecognises the assets and liabilities of the subsidiary, any Non-Controlling Interest and the other components of equity related to the subsidiary.  4.10.4 NON-CONTROLLING  INTERESTS  Non-Controlling Interests are measured at their proportionate share of the acquiree’s identifiable net assets at the acquisition date. Changes in the Group’s interest in  a subsidiary that do not result in a loss of control are accounted for as equity  transactions. As the parent holds 100% of the subsidiary’s shares, there are no Non-Controlling Interests (NCI) to recognize in the consolidated financial statements.  4.10.5 ACQUISITIONS OF NON-  CONTROLLING INTERESTS  Acquisition of Non-Controlling Interest is accounted for as transactions with equity holders. Therefore, no goodwill is recognized as a result of such transactions.  4.10.6 LOSS OF CONTROL  On the loss of control, the Group de- recognizes the assets and liabilities of the subsidiary, any Non-Controlling Interests and the other components of equity related to the subsidiary. Any surplus or deficit arising on the loss of control is recognized in statement of profit or loss. If the Group retains any interest in the previous  subsidiary, then such interest is measured at  fair value at the date that control is lost.  Subsequently that retained interest is accounted for as an equity-accounted  investee or in accordance with the Group’s accounting policy for financial instruments depending on the level of influence retained.  4.10.7 INTRA-GROUP  TRANSACTIONS ELIMINATED ON CONSOLIDATION  Intra-group balances, and income and expenses arising from intra-group transactions are eliminated in preparing the Consolidated Financial Statements.  5. (Guarantee) Ltd (NGL) and determined  that the transaction represents an internal restructuring. Although the transaction involves the transfer of inputs, processes, and outputs, there is no change in ultimate ownership or control, as the Government continues to exercise authority over the operations both before and after the transfer. While NGL operates as a company limited by guarantee with its own  governance framework, the Government  retains the power to influence key decisions, including appointments, terms of transfer, and matters relating to asset disposition in the event of liquidation. This restructuring reflects a change in legal form rather than a change in control. Accordingly, the assets and liabilities transferred to NGL have been recognized at their existing carrying amounts in accordance with the relevant accounting guidance for restructurings within entities under common control (Merger Accounting for Common Control Combinations - SoRP). No gain or loss has been recognized in profit or loss. Any difference between the carrying  values of the net assets transferred and  the agreed transfer consideration has been recorded directly in equity. RISK MANAGEMENT FRAMEWORK (i) Credit risk  Credit risk represent the risk that one party to a financial instrument will cause a financial loss to the other party by failing to discharge a contractual obligation. Credit risk mainly arises from trade debtors, and cash and cash equivalents. Cash and cash equivalents are managed and short term investment decisions are taken after proper review by the management. The credit risk from rendering courses to students is minimized by strictly monitoring attendance and degrees are offered only for students who have made full payments.  a.
